title: Viola
summary: A computed viola, outside the real spread: mostly too dark, attacks far too quick, a noisy band near 395 Hz that is the model's. E3 and Gb5 sound 11.2 and 7.3 cents sharp (finger at the equal-tempered station); C4 and Db4 have it moved to the note. Every note is a string with diameters read from photographs of a playing viola, bowed by a finite-width bow with hair compliance on the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025), driving a computed shell body (Cassavetti Stradivari outline; on E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, G3, C3 and D4 the top plate's interior thickness, the rib height and wall and the back's edge thickness of Stradivari's Gibson viola, the audio-band maple and all 279 modes of its window; on A4 still the earlier body, Johannsson's thicknesses, the registered maple and 209 modes) and its air cavity at 144 kHz. On every page but C3 and Gb5 the bow force follows bow speed at the start of the stroke (a modelling choice of player move); C4, Db4 and E3 also see the string's omitted bending modes at the bridge and the finger stop (a residual-flexibility record; nothing fitted); G3 and C3 have their after-length moved off the exact sixth by the cello's printed ratio, borrowed. D4's string carries a loss borrowed from a violin D string on a rigid monochord (Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt 2008, Q 480); the other strings carry none. Every note also carries three point masses on the shell's rib (the end blocks, a boxwood tailpiece and a Flesch chinrest, translational only: 123.3 g on E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, G3, C3 and D4, 124.6 g on A4). Every note also carries the viola's other three open strings, unbowed, on the same bridge (the three that are not sounding; on E3, Gb5, C4 and Db4 the sounding string is the one stopped by the finger). E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, C3 and G3 carry a printed damping law for the shell body (Bissinger 2008, a violin's fit borrowed: 1.0 % at 400 Hz, falling as f^-0.45), which left the earlier body's mode near 395 Hz at Q 52 against 15 to 27 printed (not re-measured on the new body); the earlier C3, D4, G3 and Db4 renders raised the wood loss 3.25 times instead, a factor with no print above 1 kHz. D4 and A4 radiate through a computed skin instead of the law (3616 triangles over 230 to 1907 Hz, loaded two-way on 68 body modes on the earlier body and on 72 on the new one). Every note plays room air from thermochemical data (NASA-9 heat capacities and pure-gas transport) in place of the named-gas row; on D4 and A4 it stacks on the skin. E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, G3, C3 and D4 were re-rendered on 11-08 on a body built from the Gibson viola's printed measurements, the audio-band maple (with the radial loss of Alkadri's plate C) and the whole window of 279 modes, and each page names what got worse first; A4 is still on the earlier body and takes the new one when its render ends.
physics_present: a computed viola shell body: the outline of the Cassavetti Stradivari viola (Library of Congress), f-holes from its caliper sheet, spruce top and maple back and ribs, a 6.5 mm mesh; on A4 plate thicknesses from Johannsson's viola table, the registered maple and the lowest 209 of the 261 modes its 15 Hz to 5 kHz window holds (the modes from about 4.05 to 5 kHz dropped); on E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, G3, C3 and D4 the top plate's interior thickness, the rib height and wall and the back's edge thickness from the printed measurements of Stradivari's Gibson viola (Hargrave 1986), the other plate thicknesses from Johannsson's table, the audio-band maple and all 279 modes of the window; the string drives it through bridge flexibility; a 3.24 L air cavity (3.16 L on E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, G3, C3 and D4) through a physical neck (an exterior neck on D4 and A4, whose mouth radiates through the skin below); dry room air (thermochemical on every note); played at 144 kHz on every note
the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13), on every page

strings with diameters measured on a playing viola (Percival 2013, Table 3.2, from photographs, about 10 %), tension and density from Guettler; the bending stiffness is derived from Percival's measured inharmonicity, because no source prints a viola string's stiffness

D4: the string's own loss, from a measurement on another string and carried to this one (DERIVED and BORROWED): loss factors eta_F = eta_B = 1/480 = 2.08e-3, so that every mode has a damping ratio of 1.04e-3, from Table VI of Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt (2008), the D string of a monochord with a rigid termination (decay time of the fundamental 0.521 s, Q1 480; the rigid termination makes the decay the string's own loss; the numbers are from the repository's hand transcription of the table); the viola's open D is the same note. Assumed: only the fundamental was measured, so the loss is constant in mode number; the paper prints Q1 and tau1, not a split between the friction and the bending terms, so the two are equal; the make and core of the viola's D string are unknown. Nothing was set by comparing with a recording. With it the grader scores D4 4 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler, as before, and 4 strict against 2; the note starts 442 ms after the bow, against 313 ms before and 604 ms in the recording

Every note: three translational point masses on the shell's rib (on E3, Gb5, C4, Db4, G3, C3 and D4 rebuilt on 11-08 for the Gibson viola's 36.3125 mm rib height in place of Johannsson's 38 mm: end blocks 15.033 g and 13.530 g, 28.930 g with the tailpiece, 123.26 g in all, the same 138, 128 and 32 rib nodes; the figures that follow are the earlier body's, which A4 still carries), the lumped masses of parts the shell does not model (no lever arm and no rotary inertia, so they cannot show a part's own modes): the upper end block 15.732 g and the lower end block 14.159 g (Johannsson's viola table, Medium: 50 x 18 and 45 x 18 mm by the 38 mm rib height; the table gives no wood, so the shell's own spruce pack at 460 kg/m3 is an assumption), the tailpiece 15.4 g added to the lower block for 29.559 g (Maderas Barber's Hill model boxwood viola tailpiece, 130 mm, ref. 11219; the same maker lists 25 g in ebony and 20 g in French boxwood, so 15 to 25 g, and the one this viola wore is unknown), and a Flesch chinrest of 79.3 g (Luthier Vidal's Wolf KH-21 listing, the only weight found for it; a Goetz Flesch viola chinrest lists 67 g with screws at Thomann), 124.59 g in all. Where they sit is a modelling choice, and no print places them: 138 rib nodes at the top end, 128 at the bottom end, and 32 on the flanks of the lower end block for the chinrest (a Flesch rest is centre-mounted over the tailpiece; a first version that put it off the centre line on the bass side was withdrawn and is on no page). Loaded response of the D string: the body's 395 Hz pole goes from one peak at 395.10 Hz, Q 75.3, effective mass 34.0 g to one peak at 390.76 Hz, Q 73.5, effective mass 41.3 g, still under the 56 to 117 g printed for a viola. On the grader D4 ties (4 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler, as before; strict 4 to 3, spectral flux leaving the strict ruler); the note is 0.4 dB louder, 2.3 and 6.1 dB louder over 1.0-1.6 and 2.4-3.5 kHz, its tenth harmonic rises 18.8 dB from 31.7 dB under the strongest, and the grader's gap grows on 13 of the 14 measures with a ruler, none by a ruler's width (the centroid gap shrinks); it plays because each mass is a sourced part of the instrument, not for a better count. Neck and fingerboard are not represented: a print gives the fingerboard's size (Johannsson: 305 mm long, 24.5 to 45 mm wide) but no neck width and no mass, and a rigid point mass cannot carry the board's own modes. Db4 carries the same masses at the same nodes (rendered on 11-06 on its bridge-row card: 3 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler against 2, strict 1 against 2; the one row that changes sides on the loose ruler, spectral flux, goes from 0.928 to 0.919 against a ruler edge of 0.925, and odd/even balance leaves the strict ruler, 1.80 to 2.82; the note is 0.5 dB louder, with +2.3, -1.9 and +4.7 dB over 1.0-1.6, 1.6-2.4 and 2.4-3.5 kHz; the grader's gap grows on 8 of the 14 measures with a ruler and shrinks on 6, none by a ruler's width; its loose rise is the one flux row crossing an edge by 0.005). The same masses sit at the same nodes on the other six notes, rendered on 11-06 on each page's own card and stops with only the body profile changed (the same 3056-node rib in the same order on every profile), and they stay on those pages whatever their counts do, as the cello's endpin and bar do, because they are sourced parts of the instrument and not a setting. What each did to its page, loose and strict counts of the real-vs-real ruler before and after: C3 5 to 3 of 14 and 5 to 3 strict (attack, 0.83 to 1.60 against an edge of 1.43, and spectral flux, 1.12 to 1.25 against 1.22, leave their rulers; the note 2.1 dB quieter; a control of the live card on the same build is byte-identical to the live page); G3 7 to 7 and 6 to 6, no row changing sides, the gap growing on 8 of the 14 measures with a ruler and shrinking on 6, none by a ruler's width (the fundamental's level swings 0.32 of its mean through the hold against 0.14, which the count does not see; the note 1.0 dB quieter; control byte-identical); A4 10 to 8 and 10 to 8 (band envelope, 8.45 to 11.91 against an edge of 10.05, and wavelet spectrum, 14.86 to 17.57 against 14.95, leave their rulers; the note 3.7 dB louder and 14.7 dB louder over 1.0-1.6 kHz; control byte-identical); E3 11 to 7 and 9 to 6 (spectrum, band envelope, harmonics and cepstral envelope leave their rulers; the note 1.6 dB louder; the live page is itself a render of the same build); Gb5 8 to 7 of 15 and 7 to 6 (harmonics leaves its ruler, 8.06 to 12.92 against an edge of 11.76, and the attack gap goes past its ruler's width, 5.05 to 5.88 against a width of 0.62; the note 1.0 dB quieter; a control of the live card on the same build is byte-identical to the live page); C4 5 to 4 and 3 to 3 (band envelope leaves its ruler, 8.25 to 10.90 against an edge of 8.68, and the cepstral envelope gap goes past its ruler's width, 7.70 to 9.06 against a width of 1.10; the note 1.9 dB quieter; the live page is itself a render of the same build)

A4: the viola's other three open strings (G3, D4 and C3) unbowed on the same bridge, each on its own bridge node of the shell (the engine takes one bridge row per string): each is the string of its own page (length, diameter measured on a playing viola, Guettler's tension, 64 modes, one polarization; D4 with the loss borrowed from a violin D string on a rigid monochord), and only the A string is bowed. They are a part of the instrument and not a setting, as the cello pages carry theirs, so the page stays whatever its count does. Rendered on 11-06 on MaroonOak's bin-ms4 (sha256 712f30720b387c4c, run in place). The posted A4 card and profile alone on that binary reproduce the live page byte for byte, so the difference is the strings and, on this note, one re-solve of a stuck port: on the previous binary this card and profile ran for 1.298 s (186880 samples), identical to this render over those samples, and then stopped on the sticking check, which bin-ms4's re-solve passes. Loose and strict counts of the real-vs-real ruler before and after: 8 to 8 of 14 and 8 to 8, no row changing sides and none crossing a ruler's width; the note +0.64 dB, the first twelve harmonics within -2.87 to +0.67 dB, harmonics-to-noise 7.70 to 5.44 (the gap to the recording, closer), the centroid 503 Hz against 1188 Hz in the recording (523 Hz before). Worse by the grader's gap to the recording: cepstral envelope 7.79 to 8.45; harmonics 14.69 to 15.56; spectrum 18.91 to 19.93; band envelope 11.91 to 12.46; brightness (centroid) 14.38 to 14.97; short-time spectrum 21.42 to 21.84; wavelet spectrum 17.57 to 17.80; pitch 4.06 to 4.09. The other strings' own pitch lines are weak on this note: D4 -72.1, C3 -95.2 and G3 -61.9 dB re the strongest line (-76.5, -95.1 and -57.4 on the previous page).

G3: the viola's other three open strings (A4, D4 and C3) unbowed on the same bridge, built as on A4 (G3 on bridge node 0, A4 on 14, D4 on 5, C3 on 119; each string of its own page; only G3 is bowed), rendered on the same binary (MaroonOak's bin-ms4) and kept on the same ground, as a part of the instrument and not on its count. The note's level changes by -11.40 dB, the second harmonic (the strongest line on the previous page, on the body's 395 Hz pole) by -29.4 dB, and the first twelve harmonics move -29.38 to +8.79 dB; the fundamental's level swings 0.65 of its mean through the hold against 0.32. Worse by the grader's gap to the recording: harmonics-to-noise 3.12 to 12.58; attack 1.54 to 2.52; partial trajectories 6.78 to 8.35; past its ruler's width: harmonics-to-noise (3.12 to 12.58, a ruler width of 7.92). A render with only the C3 string added (a diagnostic, not a page) gives the same largest changes: the second harmonic 29.1 dB lower, the level 11.0 dB lower, the 100-400 Hz band energy 13.1 dB lower, loose 12 and strict 8. The C3 string's third partial, nominally 3 x 130.81 = 392.4 Hz, lies 1.1 Hz below that harmonic; the render is consistent with that coincidence being the cause and does not show it, since no render moved or removed the partial.

a bow of finite width with hair compliance, and bridge and bow flexibility
the after-length (bridge to tailpiece) at one sixth of the speaking length; on G3 and C3 it is the sixth times 116/115, the cello's printed ratio, borrowed because no source prints a viola's

stopped notes (E3, C4, Db4, Gb5): a rigid finger on the fingerboard (Issanchou 2017), a 1e13 N/m stop and a 3.5 N press; at its equal-tempered station on E3 and Gb5, and on C4 and Db4 moved to the note by one correction of 14.5 cents, the sharpness measured on the same string's phrase renders, with the bow at 1/11 of the sounding length from the bridge

C4, Db4, E3 and Gb5: the string's omitted bending modes in series with the bridge spring and the finger stop (the engine's `residual-flexibility exact-static-green`: the exact static Green's function of the same tension, bending stiffness and pinned span, minus the retained modes' static sum; nothing is fitted and no tension, length or pitch is changed). A string seen through N retained sines cannot form the kink at a point support, so the retained modes alone are an upper bound and stopped notes come out sharp by an error that falls as 1/N; the row lowers C4 by 1.0 c, Db4 by 4.0 c, E3 by 1.2 c and Gb5 by 5.0 c. The three pages tie their predecessors on the grader (C4 5 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler, 3 strict, as before; Db4 2 of 14, 2 strict, as before; E3 11 of 14, 9 strict, as before; no row changes sides and none is worse by a ruler's width), so they play it as more physics, not for a better count. They were rendered with a build of origin 29f5b261f plus a one-line fs-lbm change (sha256 af5a271295458164), not the cap binary of the other pages; with the row left out that build reproduces the previous C4 and Db4 renders to within one 16-bit sample step and the E3 render of the card before the bow-start change byte for byte; E3's present card was not rendered on it without the row. Gb5 lost rows with the row on its one-string page (8 to 5 of 15 inside the ruler: the partial-frequency gap went from 0.06 to 15.7 c, inharmonicity B from 0.0057 to 0.60, the attack gap from 5.05 to 5.93). On its strings page, rendered with the row on the binary that rendered the strings page (a 0.5 s control of the strings card is byte-identical to the posted clip over its first 72000 samples), it ties that page: 7 of 15 inside the ruler, 6 strict, as before, no row changes sides and none is worse by a ruler's width; the note sounds 7.3 c sharp where the page without the row sounded 12.3 c. It carries the row as a correction of the string model's truncation, whatever its count. E3's attack is named: on its card before the bow-start change the row left 11 of 14 but shortened the grader's attack time from 102 to 39 ms against 558 ms in the recording; with the bow force following the speed from rest it is 134 ms (99 ms without the row), still far under the recording's 558 ms. A4, D4, G3 and C3 carry it on their cards, together with the bow-side row (`bow-residual-flexibility exact-static-green`), which the engine refuses beside the stop rows of the four stopped notes.

on D4, A4, C4, Db4, E3 and G3 the bow force follows bow speed through the start of the stroke; it is a modelling choice of player move, not a measured player's bow, and Schelleng's printed relation, that both bow-force limits for Helmholtz motion scale with the bow speed, is why a force that rises with the speed is the consistent start; the numbers are the cards' own and D4's: force 0 N at rest, then a 0.15 s ramp to the card's bow speed (0.15 m/s) and the card force, and the final force and the release are unchanged. E3 and G3 were rendered this way on 11-06 and tie the full-force pages (E3 11 of 14 inside the ruler, 9 strict against 8; G3 7 of 14, 6 strict, its attack time 158 to 202 ms against 592), so they play it for consistency, not for a better count. Gb5 was rendered this way too and lost rows (8 to 5 of 15: the partial frequencies fall apart, 0.06 to 18 c), so it keeps the full force from the start; C3 was not tried

Every note but D4 and A4: the shell body's modal damping set by a printed law in place of the wood's own loss (Bissinger 2008, total damping of free violins, band-averaged over 400-5000 Hz: 1.0 % at 400 Hz, falling as f^-0.45; a violin's fit borrowed for this viola, radiation included, no radiating skin on these six pages, the connection losses outside the law, extrapolated below 400 Hz); on the earlier body the 395 Hz pole rang down with Q 52 on D4's clip with the law (not re-measured on the new body) (G3's own second harmonic rides on the pole, so the ring-down can't be read on G3's clip, and it was not read on the other pages' clips) against 15 to 27 printed for a viola, so it is under-damped there and no factor was tuned to change that. The earlier C3, D4, G3 and Db4 renders raised the wood loss 3.25 times instead (FoggyHill's loss packs on the spruce top and the maple back and ribs; Q 26 at the pole), a factor with no print above 1 kHz, and the earlier A4, E3, Gb5 and C4 renders had the wood loss alone (Q 75 to 76 at the pole). Gb5 scores 8 of 15 inside the real-vs-real ruler with the law, as it did with the wood loss alone (7 with the 3.25 times loss), 7 strict either way, and no row changes sides: a tie, posted because the law is printed damping. On the five pages that gained it, rendered with their other strings on the bridge on the binary that rendered each strings page (a 0.5 s control of each strings card is byte-identical to its posted clip over its first 72000 samples), the counts of the real-vs-real ruler against the strings page each replaces go A4 8 to 8 of 14 loose and 8 to 8 strict; C3 4 to 3 of 14 loose and 3 to 3 strict; E3 6 to 5 of 14 loose and 5 to 3 strict; C4 4 to 4 of 14 loose and 4 to 4 strict; Db4 2 to 1 of 14 loose and 2 to 1 strict; the rows that change sides on the loose ruler: C3: band envelope (8.640 to 9.225, the loose ruler running 3.155 to 8.849); harmonics-to-noise (9.167 to 14.781, the loose ruler running 0.557 to 9.326); attack (1.940 to 0.904, the loose ruler running 0.013 to 1.432); E3: harmonics (12.835 to 11.576, the loose ruler running 7.489 to 11.595); short-time spectrum (21.826 to 22.749, the loose ruler running 18.964 to 22.682); partial frequencies (0.269 to 8.514, the loose ruler running 0.287 to 1.248); Db4: odd/even balance (2.168 to 8.570, the loose ruler running 0.117 to 3.199); gaps past a ruler's width: E3: partial frequencies (0.27 to 8.51, a ruler width of 0.96); Db4: short-time spectrum (20.91 to 22.45, a ruler width of 0.79); odd/even balance (2.17 to 8.57, a ruler width of 3.08). They carry it as a printed damping that every note but D4 and A4 has, whatever the count does, with what got worse named on each page

D4 and A4: the shell radiates through a computed skin and the printed law is gone. The skin is a closed boundary-element surface of 3616 triangles over the shell, loaded two-way on 68 body modes inside 230 to 1907 Hz (the other 141 of the 209 retained modes radiate one way), the f-holes as one opening port carrying the neck's flow and the cavity's neck an exterior neck; its load depends on the gas, so the pages as posted took one load computed for this body, skin and gas (the D4 render computed it, the A4 render read it from the store). The law's total damping already included radiation, so the skin pages drop it (keeping both would count radiation twice); the shell's own loss is then the packs' wood loss as printed, with the computed radiation damping on top. The wood's stiffness does not vary with frequency in this model. The spruce constants were fitted to the specimens' modes between 100 and 5000 Hz (Viala et al. 2020); the maple constants mix static tests (E_L, E_R), plate modes near 0.7 kHz (G_LR) and 1 MHz ultrasound (G_LT, G_RT) (Sonderegger et al. 2013, Lämmlein et al. 2020). The loss these woods show implies a slight stiffening with frequency, which would move the body's modes by up to about 22 cents across 440-2200 Hz; it is not modelled.

The rosin's temperature-dependent friction row (rosin-thermal-sw2000, applicability extended beyond its authors') was tried on A4 and does not improve it: the note sounds 12.4 cents flat and harmonics-to-noise reads 60.9 dB against the recording's 39.3, and the real-vs-real count falls from 8 to 3 of 14, so the page keeps the isothermal friction law.

the second polarization at the bridge: on every viola card the played string is two-plane (`polarizations two 1 0 1 0`) and the bridge holds only the first axis, so the vertical plane runs unsupported from nut to tail; the bow, the finger stop and the bridge are all on the first axis. A trial row on A4 that holds the bridge top along the outward normal of the notch (21.9 degrees from vertical, from a quadratic through the four bridge contacts of the Cassavetti table; shell component 24, node 14, the card's own lateral joint K 2e5 N/m and C 0.1 N s/m applied obliquely, an isotropic-joint assumption; the A4 law card as a 0.5 s prefix, read over 0.3 to 0.5 s) still changed the sound: pitch +0.23 c, the level -0.39 dB, the first harmonic by -0.44 dB, the second by -1.56, the fifth by +1.88 and the eighth by +3.46 dB. Ten times the stiffness moves the eighth harmonic by +4.68 dB and the fifth by +1.21 dB (pitch -0.02 c); ten times the damping moves the sixth by -0.35 dB and the pitch by -0.27 c. The row is set aside because the harmonics depend on its unsourced stiffness (4.68 dB at ten times it, against 3.46 dB for the row itself), and because the oblique row also loads the lateral plane (0.139 of its stiffness, 2.8e4 N/m, next to the card's 2e5 N/m); no viola page was run with it.
